The cited paragraph establishes the gathering and named participants, not a complete account of Indian founders, research topics or subsequent membership.
anglo-indian-institute.context: The institute intersects the Commonwealth organizational network and the profiles of Willingdon, Gwyer, Cecil and King-Hall.

anglo-curtis-macadam-tour.summary: Curtis and Chatham House secretary Ivison Macadam toured overseas institutes in 1938 and attended an IPR Pacific Council meeting at Princeton. Their itinerary connected Commonwealth organizations with American research and philanthropic institutions. The tour is an intersection connecting RIIA staff, Dominion institutes, the Pacific Council, CFR and philanthropy.
details: They visited the international-affairs institutes in Australia, New Zealand and Canada before attending the council meeting. Macadam had succeeded Bourdillon as Chatham House secretary in 1929. Traveling together combined Curtis’s long-standing organizing role with the institute’s current administrative representation, allowing personal links to support institutional cooperation.

Afterward they separated: Curtis addressed a Council on Foreign Relations dinner and visited the Carnegie Foundation in New York, while Macadam went to Washington to visit the Carnegie Endowment and Brookings Institution. Quigley uses the itinerary as evidence of closely connected organizations. It documents particular contacts, not a single joint program directed identically by every institution visited.
anglo-curtis-macadam-tour.context: The tour is an intersection connecting RIIA staff, Dominion institutes, the Pacific Council, CFR and philanthropy.

anglo-riia-refugees.summary: A Chatham House research program begun in 1937 produced a major refugee report edited by John Hope Simpson in 1939. Quigley situates it alongside appointments and conferences responding to Nazi persecution and the problem of stateless people. The report links institute research to refugee administration, Evian and the crises preceding the Second World War.
details: Neill Malcolm became High Commissioner for German Refugees in 1936. Makins served the British delegation at the Evian conference in 1938, then became secretary to its Intergovernmental Committee on Refugees. Stopford worked with Czechoslovak refugees in 1938–1939. These positions form related branches of the same international problem rather than a single body or appointment.

Quigley expressly says Hope Simpson was not a member of the Group, despite the institute’s sponsorship of his work. That distinction prevents the report’s authorship from being reduced to an affiliation label. The passage illustrates how research institutions and public agencies could employ expertise beyond the author’s core network while working on a problem the network considered important.
anglo-riia-refugees.context: The report links institute research to refugee administration, Evian and the crises preceding the Second World War.

anglo-frps-established.summary: At the outbreak of war the RIIA moved research resources to Oxford and formed the Foreign Research and Press Service. Toynbee directed work answering government questions, preparing special studies and summarizing the foreign press, with Curtis supporting oversight. This connects Chatham House publications and Oxford facilities to the Foreign Office’s wartime research machinery.
details: The service brought together the press-clipping collection, Information Department and much of the library in Balliol, All Souls and Rhodes House. Financing came jointly from the Treasury, colleges and Chatham House. Curtis acted as Astor’s permanent representative; assistants later included Clark, Paton, Webster and Zimmern.

Eden told Parliament in July 1941 that the Foreign Office had supplied £53,000 for the 1940–1941 financial year. Quigley interprets the arrangement as the institute becoming effectively the Foreign Office’s research section, before formal absorption. The actual mechanisms—moved collections, paid research and departmental requests—show how an outside institute supported wartime government.
anglo-frps-established.context: This connects Chatham House publications and Oxford facilities to the Foreign Office’s wartime research machinery.

anglo-frps-takeover.summary: The Foreign Office took over the Foreign Research and Press Service in April 1943, merging it with the Political Intelligence Department. Toynbee became director of the new Research Department and Zimmern deputy director, formalizing an existing wartime relationship. The merger completes the passage from independent institute research to formal wartime government service.
details: At the end of 1942 Eden wrote to RIIA chairman Astor that the government wanted complete control of the service. Previously FRPS had worked in Oxford with resources and financing from the institute, Treasury and colleges. Absorption changed its institutional position from a jointly supported research arrangement to a department within the ministry.

Quigley later follows research personnel into the department and gives Zimmern’s deputy term as 1943–1945, with Wheeler-Bennett taking that role in 1945. The event is a specific transfer of organization and responsibility. His claim that the continuing personnel made the department a network stronghold is an interpretation built on those identifiable appointments.
anglo-frps-takeover.context: The merger completes the passage from independent institute research to formal wartime government service.

anglo-indian-dyarchy-study.summary: Curtis formed an unofficial London study circle in 1911 to examine how responsible government could be extended to India. Quigley traces its discussions to the later dyarchy proposal while cautioning that the original membership cannot be established with certainty. This connects Round Table constitutional research to the Montagu–Chelmsford reforms and the Government of India Act.
details: The group initially supported a planned India chapter in Curtis’s Commonwealth work. It met fortnightly and considered assigning selected provincial functions to elected legislatures and their ministers, leaving other functions under executives responsible to the Government of India and London. India Office officials Seton, Duke and Abrahams later participated.

Chelmsford subsequently described receiving a pamphlet as if it came from an official India Office committee. Quigley compares that recollection with Curtis’s account to show the body was unofficial. The distinction is central: an informal study group’s ideas could reach senior officials and later legislation without originally carrying formal departmental authority.
anglo-indian-dyarchy-study.context: This connects Round Table constitutional research to the Montagu–Chelmsford reforms and the Government of India Act.

anglo-montagu-declaration.summary: In August 1917 Montagu announced a policy of gradually developing responsible government in India within the empire. The pledge led to his Indian visit and the Montagu–Chelmsford Report, which became the basis of the subsequent constitutional bill. The pledge links earlier study-circle discussions to a public reform process and the 1919 legislation.
details: The critical change was the promise of responsibility, not merely participation in advisory councils. Montagu’s statement called for increasing Indian involvement across administration and developing self-governing institutions. Working with Viceroy Chelmsford, he translated the policy into proposals for constitutional reform, later modified during parliamentary consideration.

Quigley places an unofficial Curtis study circle behind part of the intellectual preparation, including the dyarchy principle circulated to Chelmsford before he became Viceroy. Indian officials had initially objected to those proposals. The public declaration is a government commitment; the author’s account of how informal research prepared it remains a distinct explanation of its background.
anglo-montagu-declaration.context: The pledge links earlier study-circle discussions to a public reform process and the 1919 legislation.

anglo-india-act-1919.summary: The Government of India Act of 1919 introduced a new division of provincial responsibility and followed the Montagu–Chelmsford proposals. Quigley regards it as the period’s most important reform and examines both its public legislative path and its unofficial intellectual background. This is the legislative outcome connecting India policy declarations, dyarchy research and Selborne’s committee work.
details: Montagu’s policy announcement led to a report and a bill, which Selborne’s Joint Select Committee amended. Dyarchy allocated some provincial functions to ministers answerable through elected institutions while retaining others under existing executive authority. The act’s central-government arrangements continued, with limited change, into the mid-1940s in Quigley’s account.

The author traces the scheme back to Curtis and colleagues studying how self-government might be introduced without transferring every responsibility at once. He insists that this study circle was not an official department committee. The event therefore joins a public statute, named ministerial sponsors and an attributed account of private preparatory influence rather than presenting one undifferentiated secret action.
anglo-india-act-1919.context: This is the legislative outcome connecting India policy declarations, dyarchy research and Selborne’s committee work.

anglo-irwin-declaration.summary: On 31 October 1929 Viceroy Irwin announced Dominion status as India’s goal and a Round Table Conference to discuss constitutional reform. The declaration provoked opposition from British Liberal and Conservative leaders while opening a new negotiating framework. This intersects India constitutional reform, press decisions and the approaching three Round Table Conferences.
details: Irwin had proposed the conference on a visit to London before the Simon Commission report was complete. Reading and Lloyd George advised against the Dominion-status announcement, while Birkenhead publicly protested and Baldwin also rejected it. Quigley notes that Dawson declined Birkenhead’s letter for The Times, leading to publication elsewhere.

Irwin’s private memorandum distinguished complete constitutional freedom as understood in Britain from an Indian understanding of a constitution containing the potential for later full status. Quigley argues this ambiguity helped manage conflicting audiences. The announcement supplied a goal and a process, not an immediate grant of full Dominion powers or agreement among all Indian parties.
anglo-irwin-declaration.context: This intersects India constitutional reform, press decisions and the approaching three Round Table Conferences.

anglo-india-roundtable-first.summary: The first Indian Round Table Conference ran from November 1930 to January 1931, bringing British, princely-state and British Indian delegates into constitutional negotiations. The princes accepted federation, while Gandhi’s party refused to participate on the terms offered. This brings the India reform, princely-state and Commonwealth federation threads together in a specific negotiating session.
details: The conference had eighty-nine delegates: sixteen from Britain, sixteen from Indian States and fifty-seven from British India. Hoare and Lothian were among the British representatives; Rushbrook Williams advised the states delegation and Hailey was called for consultation. Irwin’s earlier personal discussions with princes helped prepare their participation.

Quigley regards the attempt to combine princely states and British Indian provinces within one federation as the main innovation. He also emphasizes devolution and responsibility, connecting the proposals to the Simon Commission despite claims of a complete break with it. The conference’s optimism did not settle the dispute over how quickly India would receive full powers.
anglo-india-roundtable-first.context: This brings the India reform, princely-state and Commonwealth federation threads together in a specific negotiating session.
anglo-india-roundtable-first.precisionNote: The meeting spans November 1930–January 1931; the start-month anchor is not a precise opening day.

anglo-india-roundtable-second.summary: The second Indian Round Table Conference met from September to December 1931 with broadly the same national delegations and thirty-one additional participants. Rushbrook Williams moved from advising the states group to representing the Maharaja of Nawanagar. The second session continues the constitutional negotiation and tracks the changing role of the Indian States adviser.
details: The cited list places the second session within the three-conference reform sequence and records changes in representation. As in the first session, the sixteen British delegates included eight Labour representatives and others such as Hoare, Lothian, Reading and Zetland. The additional membership enlarged the conference without replacing its basic constitutional setting.

Quigley’s paragraph principally establishes who attended and the dates, not a full narrative of each negotiation or dispute. Its significance is the continuation of a process attempting to reconcile British India and princely states within a constitutional framework. Williams’s changing role supplies a concrete link between advisory work, representation and the people involved in later reform discussions.
anglo-india-roundtable-second.context: The second session continues the constitutional negotiation and tracks the changing role of the Indian States adviser.
anglo-india-roundtable-second.precisionNote: September–December 1931 is the supplied range; the timeline begins at month precision.

anglo-india-roundtable-third.summary: The third Indian Round Table Conference met in November–December 1932 without Labour Party representatives. The British delegation shrank to twelve and included Hoare, Simon, Lothian and Irwin, now Halifax; Rushbrook Williams continued representing Indian States. The session joins the conference sequence to the committee and legislation that followed.
details: The participation list differs from the first two conferences, which included substantial Labour contingents. Quigley identifies four British delegates as members of his Milner circle and continues to track Williams through the states delegation. The narrower British representation is a concrete change in the negotiating body, not evidence that every delegate shared one constitutional position.

The session sits between earlier conferences and the government’s 1933 reform proposals and parliamentary committee. The cited passage supplies attendance and dates rather than detailed minutes of agreements. It is therefore best understood as the final stage in this conference series, connecting named personnel to the later bill while leaving individual negotiating interventions unspecified.
anglo-india-roundtable-third.context: The session joins the conference sequence to the committee and legislation that followed.
anglo-india-roundtable-third.precisionNote: November–December 1932 is the supplied range; no exact opening day is given.

anglo-india-bill-1935.summary: Samuel Hoare introduced the Government of India Bill in the Commons on 6 February 1935. He defended the reforms as an extension of responsible government, while Churchill attacked the project and drew attention to the influence of a small group of advocates. This brings the conference and committee process into parliamentary legislation while showing differing political coalitions.
details: Hoare invoked lessons from North America: Britain’s eighteenth-century mistakes and the later success of responsible government in Canada. Attlee and Herbert Samuel criticized aspects from the left; Steel-Maitland and Grigg supported him. Churchill had already denounced the bill over the BBC and sustained his opposition during the parliamentary debate.

Quigley places the introduction after years of White Papers, conferences and committee proceedings, emphasizing Hailey’s continuing advisory support to Hoare. Churchill’s comments about a few people directing large machinery matter to the author’s network thesis, but they remain an opponent’s assessment. The bill’s introduction was a public legislative step, not the final passage or immediate implementation of every provision.
anglo-india-bill-1935.context: This brings the conference and committee process into parliamentary legislation while showing differing political coalitions.

anglo-halifax-hitler.summary: Halifax met Hitler at Berchtesgaden on 19 November 1937 to discuss European changes and a possible agreement among Britain, France, Germany and Italy. Quigley analyzes the German memorandum to explain what Berlin believed Britain was prepared to tolerate. The meeting connects Halifax’s personal diplomacy to appeasement policy and the subsequent Austrian and Czech crises.
details: Halifax arranged the visit while acting as Foreign Secretary during Eden’s absence. The memorandum presented Germany as a barrier to communism and raised changes involving Austria, Czechoslovakia and Danzig. Halifax stressed peaceful methods, seeking to distinguish negotiated revision from actions that would produce a wider war.

Quigley argues that Berlin took the discussion as permission for major eastern changes and underestimated the pressure British opinion could impose if Germany used force. Chamberlain’s later letter, proposing assurances against intervention for peaceful changes, supports the author’s account of a shared policy. Intentions, the German reading and Quigley’s criticism should remain separate rather than treating the meeting as a simple signed agreement.
anglo-halifax-hitler.context: The meeting connects Halifax’s personal diplomacy to appeasement policy and the subsequent Austrian and Czech crises.

anglo-eden-replaced.summary: Halifax replaced Anthony Eden as Foreign Secretary in February 1938 after disagreement over recognizing Italy’s conquest of Ethiopia. Quigley presents the appointment as the culmination of Halifax’s growing influence over policy while he held other cabinet offices. The office change connects the Berchtesgaden visit, cabinet disagreements and the later Munich diplomacy.
details: Halifax had served as Lord Privy Seal and Lord President and accompanied Eden to Paris discussions after the Rhineland remilitarization. Quigley argues that he repeatedly restrained Eden’s respect for international obligations. Earlier support for Hoare and the 1937 Hitler visit formed part of this increasing foreign-policy involvement.

The account links the appointment to advocacy by Lothian, Dawson and Brand, who urged Chamberlain to choose Halifax despite his being a peer. Moving authority from Eden to Halifax therefore altered the department’s leadership while extending an existing policy direction. Quigley’s judgment about how the appointment enabled appeasement is an interpretation of these public offices and private lobbying.
anglo-eden-replaced.context: The office change connects the Berchtesgaden visit, cabinet disagreements and the later Munich diplomacy.

anglo-lothian-ambassador.summary: Lothian became British ambassador to the United States at the beginning of the war in Quigley’s account. His long American acquaintance and Rhodes Scholarship contacts made the appointment part of the effort to secure closer cooperation and eventual American intervention. This launches the wartime Washington thread linking diplomatic, scholarship and Anglo-American relationships.
details: As Rhodes secretary for almost fifteen years, Lothian had built personal relationships that could support diplomatic access. Quigley contrasts those advantages with his association with the Cliveden circle, which he says was little known among Americans. The appointment put a central figure in the author’s network directly in Washington.

The book treats American intervention as essential to British victory and identifies the embassy as one of several wartime institutional concentrations of associated personnel. Lothian’s role is the starting point of that Washington sequence, later continued under Halifax with economic, shipping and information missions. It is distinct from a claim that one ambassador alone could determine American policy.
anglo-lothian-ambassador.context: This launches the wartime Washington thread linking diplomatic, scholarship and Anglo-American relationships.

anglo-lothian-death.summary: Lothian’s death in December 1940 created a vacancy at an embassy considered crucial to Britain’s wartime survival. Halifax moved from the Foreign Office to Washington and retained membership of the War Cabinet, giving the post exceptional standing. This joins Lothian’s diplomacy to Halifax’s embassy and the wartime economic and information networks.
details: Quigley explains the choice through the importance of gaining American cooperation and the need for a successor with comparable political weight. Halifax remained ambassador until 1946. His retention of War Cabinet status linked overseas diplomacy directly with the highest British wartime decision-making body rather than treating the embassy as an ordinary distant legation.

The author then follows Brand, Butler, Salter and younger All Souls associates into Washington positions around Halifax. Their missions covered food, finance, shipping, information and diplomatic work. The death therefore marks both a personal loss and an institutional transition: the American policy effort continued through a different senior figure and a growing set of specialized officials.
anglo-lothian-death.context: This joins Lothian’s diplomacy to Halifax’s embassy and the wartime economic and information networks.

anglo-brand-america.summary: Brand began American wartime service in March 1941, heading the British Food Mission and later representing the Treasury. Quigley follows him through May 1946, identifying overlapping supply responsibilities and the continuing Lazard connection behind his official work. Brand’s service intersects the finance, food-supply and diplomatic strands of Britain’s American wartime effort.
details: Brand spent roughly three years with the Food Mission and two as Treasury representative. He chaired the British Supply Council in North America in 1942 and again in 1945–1946, while not resigning as Lazard managing director until May 1944. These overlapping positions show how financial experience and government supply responsibilities met in one career.

Adam Marris, Brand’s protégé and a former Lazard employee, joined the Washington embassy in 1940 and later became counselor. Quigley emphasizes these personal and professional ties around Halifax. The event establishes Brand’s period of service and duties, while the author’s classification of the embassy as a network stronghold derives from the wider concentration of associated personnel.
anglo-brand-america.context: Brand’s service intersects the finance, food-supply and diplomatic strands of Britain’s American wartime effort.
anglo-brand-america.precisionNote: The source gives March 1941–May 1946; the initial month is a service-period anchor.

anglo-berlin-washington.summary: Isaiah Berlin became First Secretary at the British embassy in Washington in 1942 after work with Wheeler-Bennett in New York. Quigley connects this move to Berlin’s academic affiliations and his friendship with the Fishers. The appointment links All Souls and New College to information work, the Washington embassy and Berlin’s later scholarship.
details: Berlin won an All Souls fellowship in 1932 after graduating from Corpus Christi and later became a New College fellow and tutor. In 1941 he went to New York to work in the Ministry of Information’s American branch with Wheeler-Bennett, remaining there less than a year before the embassy appointment.

The Washington post had recently been vacated by Adam Marris. After the war Berlin briefly held a similar post in Moscow and later lectured at Harvard. Quigley uses the sequence to show how a scholar’s college connections intersected wartime information and diplomacy. These specific movements support his network interpretation without making every academic friendship equivalent to a formal government chain of command.
anglo-berlin-washington.context: The appointment links All Souls and New College to information work, the Washington embassy and Berlin’s later scholarship.

anglo-agenda-reconstruction.summary: Agenda was founded at the end of 1942 as a quarterly devoted to postwar reconstruction. It operated under LSE auspices, with G. N. Clark as editor and editorial offices in Chatham House, connecting university research to the institute’s planning work. The journal connects wartime research with academic appointments and the effort to shape postwar policy.
details: Clark had been an All Souls member since 1912 and held the Chichele economic-history chair before becoming Regius Professor at Cambridge. Quigley explicitly describes him as close to the Group rather than a member. The journal therefore demonstrates collaboration across adjacent institutions without requiring an identical formal affiliation for everyone involved.

The author places Agenda after Toynbee’s wartime call for a broader historical understanding of postwar problems. Reconstruction became increasingly important as the war progressed, and Chatham House supplied a setting for the discussion. Quigley views the project as an attempt to influence the settlement after victory, later disrupted by Labour’s arrival in government.
anglo-agenda-reconstruction.context: The journal connects wartime research with academic appointments and the effort to shape postwar policy.
anglo-agenda-reconstruction.precisionNote: The book says the end of 1942; the year anchor does not identify an exact publication day.

anglo-salter-unrra.summary: Arthur Salter left the British Merchant Shipping Mission to become a Senior Deputy Director General of UNRRA in 1944. Quigley traces the move from wartime shipping coordination to international relief and later cabinet service. This connects the wartime shipping mission, international relief administration and Salter’s later domestic office.
details: Salter had arrived in America in 1941 to head the shipping mission, bringing experience with government shipping problems dating back to the early twentieth century. Quigley also notes his long personal acquaintance with Halifax from Oxford. The mission placed technical transport expertise inside Britain’s broader American wartime effort.

After moving to UNRRA, Salter joined the British Cabinet a year later as Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. The sequence is a career transition between organizations with distinct duties, not a claim that the shipping mission became UNRRA. Quigley’s chronology and characterization of the organization’s establishment remain the book’s account, while the appointment supplies the principal connection for this event.
anglo-salter-unrra.context: This connects the wartime shipping mission, international relief administration and Salter’s later domestic office.

anglo-labour-victory.summary: Labour’s arrival in government in 1945 disrupted the circle’s ambitions for postwar reconstruction, according to Quigley. He argues that surviving positions in newspapers, Oxford, Chatham House and the Rhodes Trust no longer had the same unified purpose. This closes the wartime planning thread and opens the question of institutional continuity after a political transition.
details: The author describes the original members as increasingly retired and the younger recruits as lacking comparable experience, conviction and contacts. He also says the Group had relatively little influence within Labour. Douglas Jay is a concrete bridge into the new government, serving Attlee after wartime posts in supply and trade administration.

Quigley’s closing assessment is sharply critical: imperial setbacks and prewar foreign-policy failures had weakened prestige even where institutional connections persisted. This is his evaluation of the network’s decline, not proof that every associated institution ceased to matter. The event marks a change of governing party and the author’s explanation of its consequences for reconstruction influence.
anglo-labour-victory.context: This closes the wartime planning thread and opens the question of institutional continuity after a political transition.
anglo-labour-victory.precisionNote: The event uses 1945 because Quigley’s stated month is inconsistent with the election chronology.

anglo-geneva-protocol-rejected.summary: Austen Chamberlain rejected the Geneva Protocol at the League Council in March 1925. Quigley treats the decision as a decisive retreat from a stronger international-security framework, linking it to Dominion opposition and British defense-policy advice. This connects League enforcement arguments, Dominion consultation, Zimmern’s dissent and the subsequent Locarno agreements.
details: Dove, Curtis, Kerr and Wilson Harris traveled to Geneva for the meeting and afterward visited Prague, Berlin and Paris. Quigley argues that associates in the Dominions could help shape opposition to additional commitments. He also cites Cecil’s account that the Committee of Imperial Defence advised rejection while promising a replacement project.

That replacement became Locarno. Quigley interprets the sequence as substituting limited guarantees for the more general enforcement contemplated in the protocol; Zimmern publicly attacked those he thought were undermining the League. The event therefore connects an official rejection to a debate within the broader circle, rather than presenting every associate as holding the same view of collective security.
anglo-geneva-protocol-rejected.context: This connects League enforcement arguments, Dominion consultation, Zimmern’s dissent and the subsequent Locarno agreements.

anglo-locarno.summary: The Locarno agreements appeared to guarantee Germany’s borders with France and Belgium through five-power commitments. Quigley argues that their reciprocal terms and legal qualifications instead constrained French action on behalf of eastern allies and left Britain room to avoid enforcement. The pacts connect the rejected Geneva Protocol to the eastern-alliance and Rhineland strands of appeasement.
details: The parties included Germany, France and Belgium with Britain and Italy as guarantors. Quigley emphasizes that guarantees could operate against either Germany or France. In his reading, French military action supporting Poland or Czechoslovakia might therefore collide with Britain’s interpretation of the pact rather than automatically gain British backing.

He attributes important legal drafting to Cecil Hurst and criticizes the agreements as less protective than their publicity suggested. The later Rhineland remilitarization becomes his test case for the guarantee’s practical value. These are interpretations of the treaty structure and subsequent policy, not the undisputed meaning of every clause accepted by all parties.
anglo-locarno.context: The pacts connect the rejected Geneva Protocol to the eastern-alliance and Rhineland strands of appeasement.
anglo-locarno.precisionNote: The source sequence locates the agreements in 1925; the timeline does not assert a particular signing day.

anglo-naval-agreement.summary: The Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 18 June 1935 accepted a German fleet up to 35 percent of Britain’s and potential submarine parity. Quigley criticizes the deal for weakening France’s strategic position while Germany rearmed. This intersects disarmament, Anglo-German accommodation and the pressure on France’s commitments in eastern Europe.
details: The source presents the agreement after British responses to German rearmament and French efforts to involve the Soviet Union in an eastern security system. It associates Simon with the policy and explains that France faced worldwide commitments and the Italian navy while its treaty allocation in major categories was smaller than the new German allowance.

Quigley argues that these circumstances made France more dependent on British naval protection and reduced its freedom to honor eastern alliances. His language is forceful, but the causal conclusion remains his geopolitical interpretation. The event links a specific negotiated naval ratio with the wider debate over Germany’s status and French security rather than claiming the ratio alone explains every later concession.
anglo-naval-agreement.context: This intersects disarmament, Anglo-German accommodation and the pressure on France’s commitments in eastern Europe.

anglo-rhineland.summary: Germany remilitarized the Rhineland in March 1936, and Britain did not enforce the earlier guarantees in the way Quigley believes was required. He regards this as the critical step allowing Hitler to strengthen his western position before moving east. The Rhineland episode links Locarno’s guarantees to the later Austrian, Czech and Polish crises.
details: The demilitarized zone had limited German forces west of the Rhine and along part of its eastern bank. Quigley argues that this exposed Germany to French action if it attacked Austria, Czechoslovakia or Poland. Once German forces and fortifications could occupy the zone, that deterrent became harder to use.

Halifax accompanied Eden to Paris discussions among the Locarno powers, with Quigley describing him as a restraint on Eden. The Times and Lothian later defended the change as correcting Germany’s unequal status. The event therefore combines a concrete military move with contrasting reactions, while the claim that it was the decisive appeasement failure is the author’s evaluation.
anglo-rhineland.context: The Rhineland episode links Locarno’s guarantees to the later Austrian, Czech and Polish crises.

anglo-munich-crisis.summary: The September 1938 Czech crisis ended in a settlement transferring territory to Germany after Chamberlain’s negotiations with Hitler. Quigley argues that diplomatic pressure and exaggerated public alarm helped obtain acquiescence while Czechoslovakia and the Soviet Union were excluded from decisive bargaining. This intersects diplomatic missions, newspaper arguments, military estimates and the Czech territorial timeline.
details: The account follows the Runciman mission, Chamberlain’s meetings at Berchtesgaden and Godesberg, and British and French pressure on the Czech government. Stopford accompanied Runciman as a technical adviser. Quigley criticizes Runciman’s contact with Sudeten representatives and the similarity between his recommendations and the eventual settlement.

The author also disputes the government’s presentation of German military superiority and interprets gas-mask distribution and trench preparations as part of a managed war scare. Those allegations and his argument about intent remain his interpretation of the cited records. The substantive event is the political sequence by which territorial concessions were negotiated and imposed, not a generic statement that appeasement occurred.
anglo-munich-crisis.context: This intersects diplomatic missions, newspaper arguments, military estimates and the Czech territorial timeline.
anglo-munich-crisis.precisionNote: September 1938 identifies the crisis as a sequence, not one single meeting or signature.

anglo-bohemia-moravia.summary: Germany’s occupation of Bohemia and Moravia in March 1939 changed the publicly advocated policy of the Milner circle, according to Quigley. The Round Table moved toward a grand alliance, while he argues Chamberlain’s circle remained more privately committed to accommodation. The occupation links the failure of the Czech settlement to alliance-building, Polish guarantees and national-service advocacy.
details: The author contrasts Chamberlain’s first Commons reaction with his later Birmingham condemnation and treats public outrage as a major constraint. In June, The Round Table called for an alliance including Britain, France, Poland and Romania, referring briefly to negotiations with the Soviet Union. Lothian had already supported an eastern as well as western alliance in an April speech.

Quigley does not portray the policy change as a retrospective admission that earlier appeasement was wrong: the journal still defended its past course. He instead identifies a new judgment about future German demands. That distinction explains why associated people could press preparedness while retaining different attitudes toward guarantees and cooperation with Russia.
anglo-bohemia-moravia.context: The occupation links the failure of the Czech settlement to alliance-building, Polish guarantees and national-service advocacy.

anglo-polish-guarantee.summary: On 31 March 1939 Chamberlain guaranteed Polish independence. Quigley emphasizes that the promise did not explicitly guarantee every existing border and criticizes the government for avoiding immediate financial and military arrangements that would give it practical force. The guarantee connects the post-Prague policy shift with alliance obligations and continuing arguments over territorial concession.
details: The Times interpreted the wording as leaving territorial revision possible without canceling the pledge, and Chamberlain accepted that distinction in the Commons. Quigley says Polish requests for a small rearmament loan and immediate staff discussions were refused. The difference between independence and territorial integrity is therefore central to the event’s meaning in this source.

He also discusses a Reuters dispatch suggesting Britain would press Poland to make concessions and Dalton’s allegation that government circles inspired it. Quigley reads the guarantee as an effort to deter war while retaining a negotiating exit. That account of motive is the author’s interpretation, distinct from the public promise and the documented wording dispute.
anglo-polish-guarantee.context: The guarantee connects the post-Prague policy shift with alliance obligations and continuing arguments over territorial concession.

anglo-national-service.summary: The 26 April 1939 national-service legislation followed a preparedness campaign associated with Amery, Grigg, Lothian and The Times. Quigley connects conscription advocacy to the circle’s changing response after Germany occupied the remaining Czech lands. This connects conscription advocacy, the post-Czech policy change and the approaching wartime mobilization.
details: Rather than publicly revisiting earlier mistakes, leading associates emphasized strengthening Britain and requiring service. Quigley contrasts this stance with Halifax’s more conciliatory speeches and notes Salter’s effort to persuade him to meet Stalin about an alliance. Preparedness and diplomatic coordination were related but contested responses to the same worsening situation.

The passage treats the act as the result of a continuing public campaign, not the creation of one individual. It also shows why the timeline intersects several lanes: arguments about appeasement, army manpower, newspaper advocacy and alliance-building developed together. The book’s statutory name and date are retained as its stated account rather than supplemented with uncited legal detail.
anglo-national-service.context: This connects conscription advocacy, the post-Czech policy change and the approaching wartime mobilization.
anglo-national-service.precisionNote: The name and day are the book’s stated formulation; no additional statutory provisions are inferred.
